adj:queer.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English queer. Doublet of quer.

adj:quick.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German quick, from Old Saxon quik, from Proto-West Germanic *kwiku, from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz; also a Central Franconian form. Doublet of keck, which see for more.

adv:quasi.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin quasi, initially officialese, later spreading into more colloquial registers.

noun:Qualm.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German quallem (“vapor, steam, smoke”). Cognate with Dutch kwalm. Usually considered a derivative of quellen (“to well, swell up”). Alternatively with the common Low and Central German development dw-, tw- → qu- (as in quer, Quark etc.) from Old Saxon dwalm (“benumbment, bemusement”), cognate of Old High German twalm, Old English dwolma. Further from …

noun:Quantum.tx: Borrowed from Latin quantum, whence also German Quant.

noun:Quark.tx: From late Middle High German twarc with the Central German development tw- → qu- (see quer), from a West Slavic language (compare Polish twaróg), from Proto-Slavic *tvarogъ. Cognate to Low German Dwarg. Doublet of Quargel.

noun:Quecksilber.tx: From Middle High German quëcsilber (also këcsilber), from Old High German quëcsilbar. Compare Dutch kwikzilver, Low German Quicksülver, English quicksilver. In this word survives the Central German form with qu-, otherwise displaced by keck (see there).

noun:Quelltext.tx: Calque of English source code, Quelle + Text.

noun:Quelle.tx: From Middle High German quelle, from Old High German quella, from Proto-West Germanic *kwalljā (“spring, well”).

noun:Qual.tx: From Middle High German quāle, from Old High German quāla, from Proto-West Germanic *kwālu, from Proto-Germanic *kwēlō. Cognate with Dutch kwaal.

noun:Quacksalber.tx: 16th century, from Dutch kwakzalver, derived from Middle Dutch quacsalven (unsure whether verb or noun). Further origin disputed, though the second component is definitely Dutch zalf (“salve”).

noun:Qualle.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German *qualle. Compare modern Low German Quall, Dutch kwal (17th c.). In spite of the earlier High German attestation, the Low German origin is agreed upon for both natural and dialectological reasons. Probably from quellen (like etymology 2 below). However, an alternative theory derives it from a word for “curdled, coagulated”, from Middle Low German quagel …

noun:Quaste.tx: From Old High German questa, from Proto-Germanic *kwastuz.

noun:Quarz.tx: From Middle High German quarz (14th c., Bohemia), probably with the Central German development tw- → qu- (as in quer etc.) from a West Slavic language (compare Czech tvrdý, Polish twardy), from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ (“hard”).

verb:quetschen.tx: From Middle High German quetzen, possibly influenced or from Old French quasser (“to break”). Cognate with Middle Low German quattern, Dutch kwetsen, Yiddish קוועטשן (kvetshn).

noun:Quinte.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quinta. Doublet of Quinta.

noun:Quarte.tx: Borrowed from Latin quarta. Doublet of Quarta.

noun:Qualität.tx: Partly via French qualité, partly directly from Latin qualitās. Compare Hunsrik Qualiteet.

noun:Quellcode.tx: Partial calque of English source code, Quelle + Code.

noun:Quittung.tx: From Middle High German quittunge, quitunge, formed quiten + -unge, the former verb deadjectival from what is now quitt.

verb:quietschen.tx: Intensive formation from quieken (“to squeak”), itself of onomatopoeic origin. See also quaken, quäken.

noun:Quartal.tx: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quārtāle n (literally “one fourth”).

verb:quälen.tx: From Middle High German queln, from Old High German quellen, from Proto-West Germanic *kwalljan, from Proto-Germanic *kwaljaną. The vowel was lengthened in modern German under the influence of the related noun Qual. Cognates include Dutch kwellen, English quell, Old Norse kvelja, and further Old Church Slavonic жаль (žalĭ, “pain”), Old Armenian կեղ (keł, “sore, ulcer”).

verb:quaken.tx: From Proto-Germanic *kwakōną (“to quack”), of onomatopoeic origin. Cognate with Dutch kwaken (“to croak”), English quack.

noun:Quadrat.tx: From Late Middle High German quadrāt(e) (ca. 1400), from Latin quadrātus m.

noun:Quitte.tx: From Middle High German quiten, from Old High German quitina, from Vulgar Latin *quidonia, from Classical Latin cotōneum, cydōnium or malum cydonium, from Ancient Greek κῠδώνῐον (kŭdṓnĭon) an elipsis from κυδώνια μῆλα, μηλοκῠδώνῐον (kudṓnia mêla, mēlokŭdṓnĭon). Cognate with Dutch kwee.

verb:quellen.tx: From Middle High German quëllen, from Old High German quëllan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwellan.

verb:quatschen.tx: Uncertain. An onomatopoeic origin (similar to klatschen or patschen) has been suggested, or a derivation from Middle High German quāt (“bad, evil”), from Old High German quat (“mud, dirt”).

verb:qualifizieren.tx: From Medieval Latin quālificāre. Compare French qualifier and English qualify.

noun:Qualifikation.tx: Borrowed from French qualification, from Medieval Latin quālificātiō.

noun:Quirl.tx: From Late Middle High German quirl, quirel, alteration of earlier Middle High German twirl, twirel, from Old High German dwiril, from Proto-West Germanic *þwiril, from Proto-Germanic *þwirilaz, related to *þweraną (“to stir”). Cognate to English twirl; also compare English quirl, curl, Middle Low German twirl, twirel, Old High German dweran.

adj:quer.tx: From Middle High German twër, dwër, quër, from Old High German twërh (“oblique”), from Proto-West Germanic *þwerh. Doublet of queer.

adv:quer.tx: From Middle High German twër, dwër, quër, from Old High German twërh (“oblique”), from Proto-West Germanic *þwerh. Doublet of queer.

verb:quasseln.tx: Late 19th c., from Low German quasseln, variant of dwasseln, iterative of Middle Low German dwāsen (“to talk nonsense”), from dwās (“dim-witted, daft”), from Old Saxon *dwās, from Proto-West Germanic *dwās. This adjective is cognate with Middle High German twās, Dutch dwaas, Old English dwǣs.

noun:Queue.tx: Borrowed from French queue. Doublet of Koda/Coda.

noun:Quappe.tx: From Middle High German quappe, kape, kope, from Old High German quappo, kwappo (“burbot, eelpout”) (also Old High German quappa, kwappa (“tadpole, burbot”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kwabbā, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷeh₂bʰ- (“to sink, submerge, dive”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Kwabbe (“burbot, eelpout; tadpole”), West Frisian kwabbe, kwab, Dutch kwab (“burbot; lobe”).

noun:Querulant.tx: 18th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin querulāns. In its broadened sense associated with unrelated quer (“cross, diagonal”).

adj:quitt.tx: From Middle High German quī̆t (“released, unencumbered, free”); derived from Latin quietare. Cognate with Dutch kwijt, English quit, French quitte.

noun:Quetzal.tx: Borrowed from Spanish quetzal, from Classical Nahuatl quetzalli (“quetzal feather”).

noun:Quentchen.tx: From Quent + -chen, from Medieval Latin quentinus, from quīntus (“fifth”).

noun:Quäntchen.tx: From the incorrect folk etymology which connected Quentchen with Quantum (“quantum”) and led to the spelling Quäntchen with ⟨ä⟩ instead of ⟨e⟩ in the 1996 spelling reform.

noun:Quader.tx: From Middle High German quāder; derived from Latin quadrum (“square”). Cognate with French carreau, Italian quadro (“square”).

adj:quicklebendig.tx: Pleonastic compound of quick (“lively”) + lebendig (“alive, lively”).

verb:quengeln.tx: Iterative to a Central German variant of zwängen (“to squeeze, force into”). Compare Central Franconian quengele, which apart from “to grizzle” also retains the literal meaning “to squeeze by pushing repeatedly”. For the onset qu- compare quer.

noun:Quiche.tx: Borrowed from French quiche, from Lorrainian Rhine Franconian Küeche, from Middle High German kuoche, from Old High German kuohho, from Proto-Germanic *kōkô. Doublet of Kuchen.

noun:Quetsche.tx: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

noun:Quinta.tx: From Latin quīnta (classis) (“fifth (class)”). Doublet of Quinte.

verb:quäken.tx: Of onomatopoeic origin; compare similar formations such as quaken (“to quack”), quieken (“to squeal”), quietschen (“to squeak”).

verb:quarren.tx: 18th century, borrowed from Low German quarren, from Middle Low German quarren, querren, quēren (“to purr, hum, coo, growl”), from Old Saxon *kwer(r)an, from Proto-West Germanic *kwer(ʀ)an. Cognate with Old High German queran (“to moan, lament, sigh”). Further origin uncertain. Perhaps onomatopoeic, or alternatively a byform of Proto-Germanic *kerzaną (“to creak”).

noun:Queer.tx: Borrowed from English queer, specifically from its noun use.

noun:Quest.tx: From Old French queste, from Latin quaesīta.

noun:Queller.tx: From Low German Queller, from Middle Low German queller, quelder. Cognate with Dutch kwelder (“salt marsh”). Probably from quellen (“to soak, swell with water”) + -er.

verb:quantifizieren.tx: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quantifico.

verb:quieken.tx: Of onomatopoeic origin; compare similar formations such as quaken (“to quack”), quäken (“to squeak”), quietschen (“to squeak”).
